terms.definition: An account is your personal space on the NEAR blockchain, like a digital identity, where you can hold tokens, interact with apps, and manage your assets securely.
A named account is a user-friendly account with a readable name, such as 'alice.near', making it easy to remember and share, unlike a random string of characters.
A sub-account is an account created under a main account, acting like a folder for organizing projects or permissions, such as 'app.alice.near' under 'alice.near'.
An access key is a digital key that grants permission to access your NEAR account, allowing actions like signing transactions or using apps, similar to a password for your account.
A function-call key is a limited access key that only allows calling specific functions in a smart contract, reducing risk by restricting what actions can be performed.
Gas is a small fee paid in NEAR tokens to process transactions or run smart contracts, covering the computational work needed on the blockchain network.
Storage staking is the practice of locking up a small amount of NEAR tokens to pay for storing data on the blockchain, like saving files or account information.
A yoctoNEAR is the smallest possible unit of NEAR token, much like a cent is to a dollar, used for precise calculations and very small transactions.
Testnet is a practice version of the NEAR blockchain where you can try out apps and transactions without using real money, using test tokens instead.
A transaction hash is a unique code that identifies a specific transaction on the blockchain, serving as a receipt you can use to track or verify it.

data.justification:
## Summary
openai/gpt-5-nano is the optimal choice for the NEAR dApp support agent, meeting all hard requirements at the lowest cost ($0.55 for the workload) while offering strong tool-calling, structured JSON output, and a 400k token context for long chat histories. Its pricing ($0.05/1M input, $0.4/1M output) undercuts all compliant alternatives, leaving budget headroom for scaling or error handling.

## Comparison
Among the 12 pre-filtered options, gpt-5-nano is the most cost-effective, with the next cheapest being gemini-2.5-flash-lite at $0.70 (27% higher). Higher-priced models like gpt-4.1-mini ($2.80) exceed the budget's value threshold without offering decisive capability gains for this use case—structured output and tool support are consistently implemented across candidates. While models like gemini-2.5-flash-lite and glm-5.3-flash offer larger contexts (1M+ tokens), gpt-5-nano's 400k context already exceeds the 200k requirement and is sufficient for extended chat histories; the cost savings outweigh the marginal benefit of extra context here.

## Recommendation
Select openai/gpt-5-nano. It delivers the best value for money by minimizing cost while reliably meeting the functional needs: it supports tools and structured_outputs, has a 400k token context, and processes the 3M input + 1M output token workload for only $0.55—well under the $3.00 budget. The model's reasoning feature (listed in its catalog entry) further enhances its suitability for a support agent that must interpret user queries, call tools like wallet lookups, and return precise JSON responses. Alternatives are either more expensive without proportional performance improvements or, like the Qwen models, have significantly higher output pricing that reduces value for this output-heavy workload.

3f4b902ee7b82babe4fc0595a3e83d33f8a3ec1a.description: Implement an ES module slugify.mjs exporting slugify(input: string, options?: { separator?: "-" | "_" | "."; maxLength?: number }): string. Rules, applied in this order: (1) Transliterate before normalizing: ß and ẞ -> ss, æ/Æ -> ae, ø/Ø -> o, œ/Œ -> oe, đ/Đ -> d, ł/Ł -> l, þ/Þ -> th, ð/Ð -> d. (2) Apply Unicode NFKD normalization (so compatibility forms decompose: ﬁ -> fi, Ⅻ -> XII, ① -> 1) and remove combining marks U+0300-U+036F. (3) Remove apostrophes (' and ’) without inserting a separator (Don't -> dont). (4) Lowercase. (5) Every run of characters outside [a-z0-9] (spaces, punctuation, existing separators, any remaining non-ASCII such as CJK) is a word boundary; words are the non-empty runs of [a-z0-9]. (6) Join words with options.separator (default "-"); never emit leading, trailing or repeated separators. (7) options.maxLength (positive integer, default unlimited): if the slug is longer, keep the longest prefix made of whole words that fits; if even the first word is longer than maxLength, return that word cut to maxLength characters. Never end with a separator. (8) Empty or whitespace/punctuation-only input returns "". (9) Idempotent: slugify(slugify(x, o), o) === slugify(x, o). (10) Throw TypeError when input is not a string; throw RangeError when separator is not one of - _ . or maxLength is not a positive integer. The automated test bounties/tests/slugify.test.mjs is the acceptance gate.

criteria.description: Explains the pipeline in order: transliteration table before NFKD, NFKD + combining-mark removal, apostrophe removal, lowercasing, word splitting on non [a-z0-9], joining with the separator, and word-boundary truncation for maxLength.

Documents edge cases: empty/whitespace-only input, repeated or leading/trailing separators, sharp s and other transliterations, compatibility characters (ligatures, roman numerals, circled digits), non-latin scripts, apostrophes, first word longer than maxLength, idempotency, and invalid options/non-string input errors.

sections.approach:
slugify.mjs is a single ES module exporting one pure function. The pipeline runs strictly in the spec's order, and each stage is chosen so the next stage sees exactly the character classes it expects.

Stage 1 — validation. Before touching the input we check types: input must be a string (else TypeError), and if options are provided they must be an object (null is treated as absent, a non-object like a number or string is a TypeError), separator must be exactly "-", "_" or "." (else RangeError), and maxLength must be a positive integer (Number.isInteger and > 0, else RangeError). Validating first means no partial work happens on bad input and error messages are deterministic.

Stage 2 — transliteration before normalization. A small literal map handles the characters that NFKD cannot fix because they are not decomposable into an ASCII base plus a mark: ß/ẞ→ss, æ/Æ→ae, ø/Ø→o, œ/Œ→oe, đ/Đ→d, ł/Ł→l, þ/Þ→th, ð/Ð→d. This is done with one pass of a global regex over a character-class of exactly those code points, so it is a single linear scan. Doing this before NFKD matters: NFKD would decompose some of these (e.g. đ → d + stroke mark) into a base plus a combining mark that stage 3 would then strip anyway, but mapping them explicitly first keeps the behavior fully specified and independent of what any given Unicode version decomposes. Note ø is deliberately mapped to plain "o" (not the slash-stripped base), per the spec table.

Stage 3 — NFKD normalization and mark removal. string.normalize("NFKD") turns compatibility forms into decomposed sequences: the ligature ﬁ becomes f+i, the roman numeral Ⅻ becomes x+i+i, the circled digit ① becomes 1 + a combining circle mark, and accented letters like é become e + U+0301. We then delete every code point in the combining-diacritical block U+0300–U+036F with a regex, which leaves the bare ASCII letters and digits and discards the accent/circle strokes. Anything that still is not ASCII after this (CJK, Cyrillic, etc.) simply falls through to stage 5 and acts as a word boundary.

Stage 4 — apostrophe removal. Both the ASCII apostrophe ' and the typographic ’ are deleted outright, with no separator inserted, so Don't → dont and Rock’n’Roll → rocknroll. This must happen before lowercasing/splitting so the two halves of a contraction stay one word.

Stage 5 — lowercase. toLowerCase() is applied after mark removal; at this point the string is essentially ASCII, so locale-independent lowercasing is safe and cheap.

Stage 6 — word splitting. Words are the non-empty maximal runs of [a-z0-9]. Every other character — spaces, punctuation, underscores, dashes, dots, emoji, any surviving non-ASCII — is a boundary. Rather than building an explicit separator-collapsing step, I match the words directly with input.match(/[a-z0-9]+/g); this inherently collapses runs of separators, drops leading/trailing separators, and returns [] (handled as "") for empty or punctuation-only input, so rules 5, 6 and 8 fall out of one regex with no special cases.

Stage 7 — joining and maxLength truncation. If there are no words the result is "". Otherwise the full slug is words.join(separator). If maxLength is set and the full slug fits, it is returned as is. Truncation is word-boundary aware: I walk the words, keeping a running length that counts each kept word plus one separator before every word except the first; a word is kept only if adding it (with its separator) keeps the total ≤ maxLength. The loop stops at the first word that does not fit, so we keep the longest whole-word prefix. If even the first word alone exceeds maxLength, the kept list is empty and we return words[0].slice(0, maxLength) — the first word hard-cut to exactly maxLength characters, which by construction never ends in a separator. Because truncation only ever cuts at word edges (or inside the single first word), the result can never end with a separator, satisfying the last clause of rule 7.

Idempotency (rule 9) is structural: a produced slug consists only of [a-z0-9] plus the chosen separator, all of which are invariant under every stage — the transliteration map does not contain any ASCII letter/digit keys, NFKD leaves ASCII untouched, there are no apostrophes or marks left, lowercasing is a no-op on lowercase text, and re-splitting a joined slug yields exactly the same word list. Hence slugify(slugify(x, o), o) === slugify(x, o) for every valid option object o.
sections.edge_cases:
- Non-string input: slugify(42), slugify(null), slugify(undefined), arrays, etc. all throw TypeError before any processing.
- Invalid separator: anything other than "-", "_", "." (e.g. "+", "", "--", a multi-char string) throws RangeError. The default (options omitted, or options without a separator key) is "-".
- Invalid maxLength: 0, negative numbers, non-integers like 2.5, NaN and Infinity all throw RangeError; only positive integers are accepted. maxLength absent or undefined means unlimited.
- options itself: omitted, undefined and null are all treated as "no options" (all defaults); a non-object such as a number or a string throws TypeError since its properties cannot be validated meaningfully.
- Empty input "" → "". Whitespace-only input (spaces, tabs, newlines) → "". Punctuation-only input like "---" or "?!?" → "", because there are no [a-z0-9] runs at all.
- Leading/trailing separators: "...Leading and trailing..." → "leading-and-trailing"; the dots at both ends produce no empty words at the edges.
- Repeated separators: "a--b__c" → "a-b-c"; a whole run of non-alphanumerics collapses into one separator. An existing slug like "already-slugged" passes through unchanged (with the default separator), which is also what makes the function idempotent.
- Existing separators of a different kind: "a_b-c.d" with separator "_" → "a_b_c_d"; the old -, _ and . all act as boundaries and are re-joined with the new separator.
- Sharp s: "Straße" → "strasse" and capital "GROSSE STRAẞE" → "grosse-strasse"; both ß and ẞ are mapped to "ss" before NFKD, so they never meet the mark-stripping stage.
- Other transliterations: æ/Æ→ae ("Æsir"→"aesir"), œ/Œ→oe ("Œuvre"→"oeuvre"), ø/Ø→o ("Ørsted"→"orsted"), đ/Đ→d ("Đakovo"→"dakovo"), ł/Ł→l ("Łódź"→"lodz" — the ó and ź lose their accents via NFKD, the ł via the table), þ/Þ→th ("Þórr"→"thorr"), ð/Ð→d.
- Compatibility characters: the ligature ﬁ NFKD-decomposes to "fi" ("ﬁnancial"→"financial"), the roman numeral Ⅻ to "xii" ("Ⅻ"→"xii"), and the circled digits ①②③ to "1", "2", "3" plus combining-circle marks that are then stripped ("①②③ ok"→"123-ok").
- Accented Latin: é, ü, ö etc. decompose under NFKD and their U+0300–U+036F marks are removed ("Héllo Wörld"→"hello-world", "Crème Brûlée"→"creme-brulee", "Ünïcödé"→"unicode").
- Non-latin scripts: characters with no ASCII decomposition (東京, Cyrillic, etc.) are simply dropped and act as word boundaries: "東京 Tokyo"→"tokyo". A string containing only such characters returns "".
- Apostrophes: ASCII ' and typographic ’ are deleted with no separator inserted: "Don't Stop Me Now"→"dont-stop-me-now", "Rock’n’Roll"→"rocknroll" (one word, not rock-n-roll).
- maxLength truncation on a word boundary: "The quick brown fox jumps" with maxLength 15 → "the-quick-brown" (adding "fox" would need 19); "The quick brown fox" with 9 → "the-quick"; "one two" with 7 → "one-two" (fits exactly, separator included in the count); "one two" with 6 → "one" (the full slug is 7, one over).
- First word longer than maxLength: "Supercalifragilistic word" with maxLength 5 → "super" — the first word is hard-cut to 5 characters rather than returning "". This cut can never end in a separator because the word consists only of [a-z0-9].
- maxLength with a custom separator: "Crème Brûlée Recipe" with separator "_" and maxLength 12 → "creme_brulee" ("creme_brulee_recipe" is 19, and adding "recipe" would exceed 12).
- maxLength larger than the slug: the slug is returned unchanged, no padding or trailing separator.
- Never a trailing separator: truncation only removes whole trailing words (separator included in the accounting) or cuts inside the first word, so no result ever ends with "-", "_" or ".".
- Idempotency: for every case the test re-slugs its own output with the same options and requires equality; since a slug contains only [a-z0-9] and the separator, every pipeline stage is a no-op on it, so slugify(slugify(x, o), o) === slugify(x, o).

sections.approach: The implementation follows a strict pipeline as specified in the bounty description, ensuring each rule is applied in order. First, transliteration is performed using a mapping table for specific characters (ß, ẞ, æ, Æ, ø, Ø, œ, Œ, đ, Đ, ł, Ł, þ, Þ, ð, Ð) to their ASCII equivalents before any normalization, as required. This ensures characters like 'ß' become 'ss' early. Next, Unicode NFKD normalization decomposes compatibility forms (e.g., ligatures, roman numerals, circled digits) into base characters and combining marks. Combining marks in the range U+0300-U+036F are then removed, leaving only the base characters. Apostrophes (both straight ' and curly ’) are removed without inserting separators, so contractions like "Don't" become "dont". The string is lowercased to meet the [a-z0-9] character set requirement. Word boundaries are identified by splitting on any character outside [a-z0-9], including spaces, punctuation, and non-ASCII characters (e.g., CJK scripts), which are effectively dropped. Words are defined as non-empty runs of [a-z0-9]. These words are joined with the specified separator (default '-'), ensuring no leading, trailing, or repeated separators. If maxLength is provided, the slug is truncated to fit: if the slug exceeds maxLength, the longest prefix of whole words that fits is used; if even the first word is longer than maxLength, that word is cut to maxLength characters, and no trailing separator is emitted. Empty or whitespace/punctuation-only inputs return an empty string. Idempotency is guaranteed by ensuring the pipeline produces a stable output that, when re-slugified with the same options, yields the same result. Input validation throws TypeError for non-string inputs and RangeError for invalid separator or maxLength values.
sections.edge_cases: Key edge cases handled include: 1) Empty strings or inputs containing only whitespace/punctuation return an empty string. 2) Repeated separators (e.g., 'a--b') are collapsed into a single separator. 3) Leading and trailing separators are removed entirely. 4) Transliteration of specific characters like sharp s (ß/ẞ -> ss), ligatures (æ/Æ -> ae, ø/Ø -> o, œ/Œ -> oe), and others (đ/Đ -> d, ł/Ł -> l, þ/Þ -> th, ð/Ð -> d) is applied correctly. 5) Unicode compatibility characters (e.g., ligatures like 'ﬁ' -> 'fi', roman numerals like 'Ⅻ' -> 'XII', circled digits like '①' -> '1') are decomposed via NFKD and normalized. 6) Non-Latin scripts (e.g., CJK characters) are treated as word boundaries and dropped, leaving only ASCII [a-z0-9] runs. 7) Apostrophes (both straight and curly) are removed without adding separators, so "Rock’n’Roll" becomes "rocknroll". 8) When maxLength is set and the first word exceeds it, the word is truncated to maxLength characters (e.g., "Supercalifragilistic" with maxLength=5 becomes "super"). 9) Idempotency is maintained: slugifying the output again with the same options yields the same string. 10) Invalid inputs throw appropriate errors: TypeError for non-string input, RangeError for separator not in ['-', '_', '.'] or maxLength not a positive integer.

items.rationale: Isolates the AI agent's activities to a dedicated sub-account (e.g., agent.main-account.near), limiting financial and operational risk if the agent is compromised. This prevents the parent account's assets from being directly exposed, containing any breach to the sub-account's balance and permissions only.
items.title: Use Sub-Accounts for Agent Isolation

items.rationale: Replaces full-access keys with function-call keys that restrict the agent to specific contract methods and a set allowance, preventing unlimited transactions if the key is leaked. This enforces least-privilege access, reducing the impact of key exposure to predefined actions and spending caps.
items.title: Replace Full-Access Keys with Function-Call Keys

items.rationale: Sets a precise allowance (in yoctoNEAR) on function-call keys to cap the agent's spending per key, avoiding drain of the sub-account balance due to bugs or malicious actions. This ensures the agent operates within a strict budget, mitigating financial risks from excessive or erroneous transactions.
items.title: Set Strict Allowance Limits on Function-Call Keys

items.rationale: Limits the function-call key to only necessary contract methods (e.g., ['submit_action']), avoiding wildcards like ['*'] to reduce attack surface. This prevents the agent from calling unauthorized methods, such as withdrawal functions, even if the key is compromised, enforcing method-level security.

sections.checklist:
1. **Use Sub-Accounts for Agent Isolation**: Create a dedicated sub-account (e.g., agent.main-account.near) for each AI agent to isolate its activities from the main account. Rationale: This limits blast radius if the agent is compromised; only the sub-account's funds and permissions are at risk, protecting the parent account's assets. Use near-cli-rs: `near create-account agent.main-account.near --masterAccount main-account.near --initialBalance 5`. Ensure the sub-account name follows NEAR's naming conventions.
2. **Replace Full-Access Keys with Function-Call Keys**: Never store full-access keys on the agent. Instead, create a function-call access key that restricts the agent to specific contract methods and an allowance. Rationale: Full-access keys allow unlimited transactions, posing a severe risk if leaked; function-call keys enforce method-level and spending limits. Use near-api-js: `account.addKey(publicKey, contractId, methodNames, allowance)` where methodNames is an array like ['interact'] and allowance is a string like '10000000000000000000000' (0.01 NEAR).
3. **Set Strict Allowance Limits on Function-Call Keys**: Define a precise allowance (in yoctoNEAR) for each function-call key to cap the agent's spending per key. Rationale: Prevents drain of the sub-account balance due to bugs or malicious actions, ensuring the agent cannot exceed its allocated budget. Use near-cli-rs: `near add-key agent.main-account.near --contract-id contract.near --method-names interact --allowance 0.01`. Monitor and adjust allowances based on usage patterns.
4. **Restrict Methods on Function-Call Keys**: Limit the function-call key to only the necessary contract methods (e.g., ['submit_action', 'vote']). Avoid wildcards like ['*']. Rationale: Reduces attack surface by preventing the agent from calling unauthorized methods, such as withdrawal or administrative functions, even if the key is exposed. Use near-api-js: `account.addKey(publicKey, 'contract.near', ['submit_action'], allowance)`.
5. **Remove Full-Access Keys from Sub-Accounts**: After creating a function-call key, delete any full-access keys associated with the sub-account to eliminate backdoors. Rationale: Full-access keys bypass all restrictions; removing them ensures the agent operates solely under the constrained function-call key. Use near-cli-rs: `near delete-key agent.main-account.near <public-key>`.
6. **Implement Key Rotation for Compromise Recovery**: Periodically rotate function-call keys by adding a new key with the same restrictions and deleting the old one. Rationale: Mitigates long-term risks from key leakage or brute-force attacks, maintaining security over time. Use near-cli-rs: Add new key: `near add-key agent.main-account.near --contract-id contract.near --method-names interact --allowance 0.01`, then delete old key: `near delete-key agent.main-account.near <old-public-key>`.
7. **Secure Sub-Account Deletion Procedures**: Plan for safe deletion of sub-accounts when agents are decommissioned, transferring remaining funds back to the main account. Rationale: Prevents abandoned accounts from becoming targets or losing funds. Use near-cli-rs: `near delete agent.main-account.near beneficiary-account.near`, ensuring the beneficiary account exists and has sufficient storage.
8. **Audit Agent Transactions Regularly**: Monitor the sub-account's activity using NEAR Explorer or indexers to detect anomalies. Rationale: Early detection of unauthorized transactions or allowance exhaustion allows quick response, such as key rotation or pausing the agent. Use near-api-js: `account.viewAccount(accountId)` to check balance and access keys.
9. **Validate Contract Interactions Before Deployment**: Test agent interactions on testnet with the same security configurations as mainnet. Rationale: Catches misconfigurations (e.g., overly permissive methods) in a safe environment, reducing mainnet risks. Use near-cli-rs testnet commands: `near --networkId testnet create-account agent.test.near`.
10. **Use Multi-Signature for Critical Operations**: For high-value agents, require multi-signature approvals from the main account for actions like allowance increases or key changes. Rationale: Adds an extra layer of security, preventing single points of failure in autonomous systems. Implement via smart contracts or NEAR's multi-sig tools.

It focuses on mitigating risks associated with agent autonomy, such as unauthorized transactions, excessive spending, and key compromise. By following these steps, teams can ensure their agents operate within strict, predefined boundaries, minimizing attack surfaces while maintaining functionality. The checklist emphasizes concrete commands using near-cli-rs and near-api-js, with references to official NEAR documentation for deeper exploration.

sections.checklist:
1. **Use Function-Call Access Keys Instead of Full-Access Keys**
   - Rationale: Full-access keys allow unlimited transactions, posing a severe risk if compromised. Function-call keys restrict the agent to specific contract methods with a defined allowance, limiting potential damage. Use near-cli-rs to create a function-call key: `near account add-key <sub-account> --contract-id <contract> --method-names <method1,method2> --allowance <amount>`. In near-api-js, generate a key pair and add it via `account.addKey(publicKey, contractId, methodNames, allowance)`.

2. **Set Strict Allowance Limits on Function-Call Keys**
   - Rationale: Without an allowance limit, a compromised key could drain the sub-account's balance via repeated transactions. Specify a small, sufficient allowance for expected operations. Update allowance with near-cli-rs: `near keys set-allowance <sub-account> --access-key <public-key> --allowance <new-amount>`. In near-api-js, use `account.updateAccount({ allowance: newAmount })` after retrieving the key.

3. **Restrict Methods to Only Necessary Contract Functions**
   - Rationale: Broad method permissions (e.g., `*`) allow the agent to call any contract method, increasing attack surface. Limit to exact methods required. When adding a key, specify methods: in near-cli-rs, use `--method-names transfer,execute`; in near-api-js, pass an array like `['transfer', 'execute']` to `addKey`. Regularly review and adjust methods as needed.

4. **Remove Full-Access Keys from Sub-Accounts After Setup**
   - Rationale: Full-access keys are often used during creation but should be deleted to prevent misuse. Ensure only function-call keys remain. Delete a key with near-cli-rs: `near account delete-key <sub-account> <public-key>`. In near-api-js, call `account.deleteKey(publicKey)`. Verify keys with `near account view-keys <sub-account>` or `account.getAccountKeys()`.

5. **Implement Key Rotation for Compromised or Stale Keys**
   - Rationale: Regular key rotation reduces the impact of key leakage. Replace old keys with new ones, updating allowances and methods. Rotate by adding a new function-call key, testing it, then deleting the old key. Use near-cli-rs: `near account add-key` for the new key, then `near account delete-key` for the old. In near-api-js, sequence `addKey` and `deleteKey` calls, ensuring the new key is active first.

6. **Control Sub-Account Creation with Parent Account Policies**
   - Rationale: Unrestricted sub-account creation can lead to spam or resource exhaustion. Use the parent account to enforce naming conventions and limits. Create sub-accounts via near-cli-rs: `near create-account <sub-account> --masterAccount <parent> --initialBalance <amount>`. In near-api-js, use `parentAccount.createAccount(subAccountId, publicKey, initialBalance)`. Set policies in the parent's contract to validate sub-account names.

7. **Enable Sub-Account Deletion for Cleanup and Recovery**
   - Rationale: Orphaned sub-accounts may hold funds or keys that pose lingering risks. Implement deletion procedures to remove unused accounts. Delete with near-cli-rs: `near delete-account <sub-account> --beneficiary-id <parent>`. In near-api-js, call `subAccount.deleteAccount(parentAccountId)`. Ensure all keys are removed first and transfer any remaining balance.

8. **Monitor Transactions and Key Usage for Anomalies**
   - Rationale: Proactive monitoring detects unauthorized activity early, allowing rapid response. Use NEAR Explorer or indexers to track transactions. In near-api-js, fetch transactions: `account.getAccountDetails().then(details => details.transactions)`. Set up alerts for unexpected method calls or allowance breaches, and log all agent interactions.

9. **Validate Contract Inputs and Handle Errors Gracefully**
   - Rationale: Malicious or malformed inputs can cause contract failures or unintended state changes. The agent should sanitize inputs and implement retry logic. In near-api-js, use try-catch blocks around contract calls: `try { await contract.method.methodName(args).gas(gasAmount).transact() } catch (error) { logError(error) }`. Ensure the contract includes input validation to reject invalid data.

10. **Test Security Configurations in Testnet Before Mainnet Deployment**
    - Rationale: Misconfigured keys or allowances can lead to immediate exploits in production. Use testnet to verify limits and behavior. Deploy with near-cli-rs: `near --network testnet create-account` and test transactions. In near-api-js, connect to testnet: `new Near({ networkId: 'testnet', ... })`. Simulate attack scenarios to confirm restrictions hold.

sections.approach: I'll implement slugify() as a pipeline of transformations applied in the exact order specified. First, transliteration using a map for the specific characters (ß, ẞ, æ, Æ, ø, Ø, œ, Œ, đ, Đ, ł, Ł, þ, Þ, ð, Ð). This must happen before NFKD normalization to ensure proper handling. Second, apply NFKD normalization to decompose compatibility characters, then remove combining marks (U+0300-U+036F) using a regex. Third, remove apostrophes (both straight and curly) without inserting separators. Fourth, convert to lowercase. Fifth, split into words: identify runs of [a-z0-9] as words, with any character outside that set treated as a word boundary. Sixth, join words with the separator (default '-'), ensuring no leading, trailing, or repeated separators. Seventh, handle maxLength: if the slug exceeds maxLength, find the longest prefix of whole words that fits; if the first word alone exceeds maxLength, truncate it to maxLength characters. Eighth, handle empty or whitespace-only input by returning an empty string. Ninth, ensure idempotency by verifying that the pipeline produces the same output when reapplied. Tenth, validate input type and options, throwing appropriate errors. The implementation will be pure, deterministic, and efficient using string methods and regexes.
sections.edge_cases: Key edge cases: 1) Empty string or whitespace/punctuation-only input returns empty string. 2) Repeated separators in input should collapse to single separators in output. 3) Leading/trailing separators should be removed. 4) Transliteration of sharp s (ß/ẞ) to 'ss' and other specified characters. 5) Compatibility characters like ligatures (ﬁ -> fi), roman numerals (Ⅻ -> XII), and circled digits (① -> 1) via NFKD. 6) Non-Latin scripts (e.g., CJK) are removed as they become non-[a-z0-9] characters. 7) Apostrophes removed without separator insertion. 8) When maxLength is less than the first word length, truncate the first word. 9) Idempotency: slugify(slugify(x)) must equal slugify(x). 10) Invalid input (non-string) throws TypeError. 11) Invalid separator or maxLength throws RangeError. 12) Mixed separators in input (e.g., 'a_b-c.d') normalize to the chosen separator. 13) Case where maxLength exactly matches a word boundary. 14) Input with only separators returns empty string. 15) Combining marks removal after NFKD ensures clean base characters.
